Title: [from] New Moons of Saturn
Author: by Nick D’Alto
Content: Tiny, lumpy, and whizzing around their planet in all directions. And not just `text(one)` or `text(two)` of them, but an entire swarm. Welcome to the surprising new moons of `text(Saturn)`.

Astronomer Edward Ashton led the team that recently discovered an astonishing `63` tiny new natural satellites orbiting around the `text(sixth)` planet from the sun. His findings pushed `text(Saturn)` past `text(Jupiter)` for the most moons in our solar system. No one has ever found this many moons before. . . .

Astronomers have been finding moons in orbit around `text(Saturn)` for `text(centuries)`. It began not long after the introduction of the telescope, which happened in `1608`. Dutch science pioneer Christiaan Huygens discovered the `text(first)` known moon of `text(Saturn)` in `1655`; it was named Titan.

By using ever-more powerful instruments over the `text(years)`, astronomers found nearly a `text(hundred)` more moons. So, why expect to find even more than that? “Based on a planet’s size and other traits, we can estimate how the moons that orbit around that planet should vary in size and what percentage are big and small,” Ashton explains. “For `text(Saturn)`, smaller moons were still missing from the total.”

But these missing moons around `text(Saturn)` would prove difficult to spot. “They’d be very small and dim,” Ashton says. “Plus, they’d be moving rapidly, so they wouldn’t stay in the same place long.”

Their movements make the moons too faint to appear in a still photograph, even when taken using a powerful telescope. And longer exposures would just show nearly meaningless streaks. “Even the Voyager and Cassini satellites, which flew past `text(Saturn)`,” Ashton says, “failed to notice these moons.”

To finally spot these elusive orbiters, Ashton and his team used a cutting-edge technique called shift and stack. This involved `text(first)` taking many images through the telescope of regions around `text(Saturn)` where the moons might be. [The team] obtained a total of `44` images, for `text(each three-hour period)`. Then, based on how the moons should be moving, `text(each image)` was shifted. So, the spot where moons should appear landed in the same place in `text(each frame)`.

There was still nothing to see. `text(Each moon)` image remained too dim. But the researchers overlapped the images and carefully aligned them. These fuller pictures revealed moons that were bright enough to see! “This method had been used before to find moons around other planets,” Ashton says, “but never around a giant planet like `text(Saturn)`, where there is so much more space to explore.”

The moons these images captured are uncannily small. They are miniature worlds, measuring just a few `text(miles)` . . . across. They are shaped like lumpy potatoes, as they lack sufficient mass for their gravity to make them round. They orbit very far from `text(Saturn)` itself, from `text(six)` to `text(18 million miles)` (`10` to `text(29 million km)`) out. On average, they are about `50` times farther away than our moon is positioned from `text(Earth)`. Their orbits are unusual in other ways, too. They’re extremely elongated and slanted compared to the planet’s orbit. Different moons of `text(Saturn)` revolve in different directions. And some moons follow `text(one)` another in virtually the same orbit. . . .

These new moons make `text(Saturn)` an even more fascinating place. `text(Saturn)` is most famous for its distinctive rings, which are made from `text(millions)` of shimmering ice crystals. Ten times the size of `text(Earth)` and `10` times as far from the sun, `text(Saturn)` is a “gas giant” made of mostly hydrogen and helium. This means the planet has no solid surface. Because it is orbited by so many moons, some scientists liken it to a kind of “mini solar system.”

The newly found moons also change the way we think about moons themselves. They remind us that not every moon is like our moon, or the other, larger regular `text(ones)`. “The larger moons exert the greatest effects on their planets,” Ashton says. “But in terms of numbers, the most common moons in the solar system are these tiny `text(ones)`.”
